title: Two Pointers
summary: Scan from both ends, or read and write in one pass

steps.title: The slow way first
steps.body: Sorted array, find two numbers that add up to target. The obvious way tries every pair. That's about n² / 2 checks, far too many when n is 100,000.

steps.prompt: n = 100,000. About how many pairs does the slow way check?
steps.why: n² / 2 = 10¹⁰ / 2. At about 10⁸ simple steps a second, that's close to a minute.

steps.title: One pointer at each end
steps.body: Start l at the smallest number and r at the biggest. Too small? Move l right. Too big? Move r left. Each step rules out one number for good, so the scan is O(n).

frames.note: l meets r. No pair adds up to 8

steps.title: Why moving is safe
steps.body: Sum too small? a[l] is too small even next to the biggest number left, a[r]. So a[l] can never be part of the answer, and dropping it loses nothing. Too big works the same way for a[r].

steps.prompt: a = [1, 3, 4, 6, 9], target = 7. The first sum is 1 + 9 = 10. What moves?
steps.why: 10 is too big. 9 is too big even with the smallest number left, so drop it.

steps.prompt: a = [2, 5, 7, 11, 15], target = 18. How many sums get checked, counting the one that matches?

steps.why: Stop when they meet: a number can't pair with itself.
Check too small, then too big. Anything else is a match.

steps.prompt: What does this method rely on?
steps.why: The moves are only safe because a[l] is the smallest and a[r] the biggest of what's left.

steps.prompt: The input isn't sorted, so you sort it first. Total time?
steps.why: Sorting costs O(n log n). The scan after it is only O(n).

steps.prompt: Match each approach to its time
steps.why: Sorting is the most expensive part once you use two pointers.

steps.title: Both pointers go forward
steps.body: r reads every element. w marks where the next element you keep goes. You filter the array in place, in one pass, with no extra memory.

frames.note: a[r] = 1 equals the last kept value. Skip it
a[r] = 2 is new. Write it at w, then w++
a[r] = 2 equals the last kept value. Skip it
a[r] = 3 is new. Write it at w, then w++
Done: the first w = 3 values are 1, 2, 3

steps.prompt: Run it on a = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]. What is w at the end?
a = [4, 4, 4, 4]. What is w at the end?
steps.why: Every value equals the first one, so only one is kept.

steps.title: Move zeros to the end
steps.body: Same idea: every non-zero number is swapped into slot w. The zeros pile up behind it, and the non-zeros keep their order.

frames.note: 1 isn't zero. Swap it into w, then w++
3 isn't zero. Swap it into w, then w++

steps.why: Non-zeros keep their order and fill the front; zeros end up at the back.
Zeros are skipped; everything else moves to the front.
Start the writer at 0, read everything, keep only non-zeros.

steps.prompt: Two pointers, so why is this O(n) and not O(n²)?
steps.why: Each pointer moves at most n times in total, so the work is at most 2n steps.

steps.prompt: Which problem fits reader and writer?
options: Remove every space from a string in place
Find two numbers with sum k
Find x in a sorted array
steps.why: Keep every character that isn't a space, in one forward pass.

steps.prompt: Match each part to its job
steps.why: The reader looks at everything; the writer only moves when something is kept.
